newsitem.title: USA: Out of question to weaken EMU criteria - de Silguy.
newsitem.headline: Out of question to weaken EMU criteria - de Silguy.

text.p: European Union Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy on Monday ruled out the possibility of a weakening of the entry criteria for monetary union.

"It is out of the question to weaken the conditions or add new conditions," he said at an informal briefing for reporters on the fringe of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank semi-annual meeting.
De Silguy was responding to a question about the implications the French elections might have on the EMU guidelines and timetable.
French Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin said on Monday that if his party won the upcoming parliamentary elections, it would put conditions on France's entry into the European single currency.
"Elections are a permanent state in Europe," de Silguy noted. "We cannot adapt the euro timetable to national elections."

The EU official also said that he had no doubt about France and Germany meeting the strict Maastrict criteria for EMU. "I have no fear about it, France and Germany will meet the criteria," he said. He said the decision on which countries will qualify for EMU in the first wave would take into account structural reform plans beyond 1997.

"Each member state has to achieve a high degree of sustainable convergence," he said. If countries used one-off measures in 1997, it will be necessary for them to show "structural measures" toward future fiscal consolidation, he said.
De Silguy said the latest European Union forecasts for Italy were not grounds for its exclusion from the first wave of EMU.
The European Commission forecast on Wednesday that Italy's 1997 deficit would be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product, just wide of the ceiling set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
"The examination will take place next year on real 1997 figures, not forecasts," he said. "Our forecasts are not a reason to say Italy will be outside EMU."
The announcement of the method for fixing foreign exchange rates among EMU members is expected to come before January 1999, the planned date of the euro's launch.
"The decision has not been taken on the method of fixing exchange rates," de Silguy told reporters. "It will be announced before the first of January of 1999."
